overview:
In Jainism, a "Shravika" (Sanskrit: śrāvikā; Prakrit: sāviā) is a female lay follower, the counterpart to the male "Shravaka" (śrāvaka). Together, Shravakas and Shravikas constitute the lay community (gṛhastha) within the fourfold Jain saṅgha, which also includes male ascetics (muni/śramaṇa) and female ascetics (āryikā/sādhvī). The term derives from the verbal root "śru"—to hear—indicating one who listens attentively to the teachings (śruta) of the Jinas and their authorized teachers. A Shravika is therefore not merely a passive listener, but a practitioner who receives, internalizes, and lives according to the Jain dharma while remaining in household life.

Classical Jain texts describe two broad paths of spiritual discipline: the path of complete renunciation (mahāvrata) for ascetics, and the path of partial renunciation (anuvrata) for householders. A Shravika belongs to the second category—she practices partial abstinence from harmful actions, guided by vows that are adapted to the realities of family, social, and economic responsibilities. Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya and Ratnakaraṇḍa Śrāvakācāra explicitly define Shravakas and Shravikas as those who follow the path of "partial abstinence" (deśa-virati), in contrast to ascetics who observe total abstinence (sarva-virati). This distinction does not imply a lesser spiritual dignity; rather, it recognizes graded paths suited to different capacities and life situations.

The core ethical framework for a Shravika is the set of twelve lay vows (dvādaśa-vrata), elaborated in texts such as Ratnakaraṇḍa Śrāvakācāra and later Shravakācāra treatises. These include five minor vows (anuvrata) corresponding to non-violence (ahiṃsā), truthfulness (satya), non-stealing (asteya), sexual restraint (brahmacarya), and non-possessiveness (aparigraha); three guṇa-vratas (vows that enhance and refine the minor vows, such as limiting directions, activities, and consumables); and four śikṣā-vratas (disciplinary or training vows that cultivate regular practice of restraint, charity, and meditation). For Shravikas, these vows are undertaken with explicit attention to the ethical challenges of domestic life—care for family, management of resources, and participation in social networks—while striving to minimize violence, deceit, greed, and attachment.

In addition to the twelve vows, Jain tradition prescribes six essential duties (ṣaḍ-āvaśyaka) for Shravikas and Shravakas alike: worship of the Pañca-Parameṣṭhi (five supreme beings), reverent listening to and following the teachings of saints, study of scriptures (svādhyāya), periodic meditation (sāmāyika), disciplined conduct in daily life (samyama), and fourfold charity (dāna) in the forms of food, medicine, knowledge, and fearlessness (abhaya). These practices are understood as daily anchors that help lay followers integrate Jain values into ordinary routines. For a Shravika, this often means weaving devotion, scriptural study, and acts of compassion into the rhythms of household work, caregiving, and community participation.

Historically, Shravikas have played a significant role in sustaining Jain communities: supporting temples and monastic orders, transmitting rituals and stories within families, and modeling ethical living in social and economic spheres. In inscriptions and narrative literature, the term śrāvikā appears as a designation for female lay worshippers who sponsor religious activities, undertake fasts, and cultivate right faith (samyag-darśana). While doctrinal texts tend to describe the lay path in gender-neutral or male-coded language ("śrāvaka"), the lived tradition recognizes Shravikas as indispensable participants in the fourfold saṅgha.

From a doctrinal perspective, the spiritual goal of a Shravika is ultimately the same as that of an ascetic: liberation (mokṣa) through the purification of the soul and the shedding of karmic bondage. The difference lies in the method and pace. By practicing the twelve vows, the six essentials, and additional observances such as graded renunciation (pratimā) and, in some cases, the final fast of sallekhanā under proper guidance, a Shravika gradually reduces passions (kaṣāya), cultivates equanimity, and prepares herself—if conditions permit—for deeper renunciation in this or future lives. Classical Digambara and Śvetāmbara Shravakācāra texts emphasize that sincere lay practice, whether by Shravaka or Shravika, is a valid and respected path of spiritual progress, provided it is grounded in right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct.

Modern discussions of Shravika identity also engage questions of gender, social roles, and changing economic structures. While traditional descriptions often assume a domestic, family-centered role for Shravikas, contemporary Jain communities include women who participate in professional life, leadership in religious organizations, and advanced scriptural study. The underlying ethical framework—non-violence, truth, non-stealing, sexual responsibility, and non-possessiveness—remains constant, but its application is interpreted in dialogue with new contexts. Across these variations, the defining feature of a Shravika is her commitment to listening to the dharma, reflecting on it critically, and embodying it in thought, speech, and action while living as a lay follower.

primary_sources.title: Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya
primary_sources.author: Acharya Amritchandra (Digambara tradition)
primary_sources.original_text:
संयताः शुद्धचैतन्ये यतयः सर्वविरताः ।
य एते देशविरतिं चरन्ति ते श्रावका इति ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
saṃyatāḥ śuddha-caitanye yatayaḥ sarva-viratāḥ |
ya ete deśa-viratiṃ caranti te śrāvakā iti ||
primary_sources.translation: Ascetics who are restrained and established in pure consciousness observe complete abstinence. Those who practice the path of partial abstinence are called Shravakas.
primary_sources.notes: This verse (often cited as Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya 41) distinguishes between ascetics (sarva-viratāḥ) and lay followers (śrāvakāḥ) on the basis of complete versus partial abstinence. Although the wording uses the masculine plural "śrāvakāḥ", traditional exegesis applies the category to both Shravakas and Shravikas, as members of the lay community who follow deśa-virati. The text is a Digambara doctrinal treatise (Tier A/B) that systematically explains the path to spiritual attainment for both ascetics and householders.

primary_sources.title: Ratnakaraṇḍa Śrāvakācāra
primary_sources.author: Acharya Samantabhadra (Digambara tradition)
primary_sources.translation: The dharma of a Shravaka is characterized by right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct.
primary_sources.notes: Ratnakaraṇḍa Śrāvakācāra is a foundational Digambara text on the conduct of lay followers. It expounds the twelve vows, the nature of right faith, and the graded stages of lay renunciation (pratimā). While the title and many passages speak of "śrāvaka" in the masculine, commentarial tradition and community usage extend its prescriptions to Shravikas as well. The text is widely regarded as authoritative for lay ethics (Tier A/B), though exact wording and verse numbering can vary across editions.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Acharya Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi (accepted by both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions)
primary_sources.original_text:
अहिंसासत्यास्तेयब्रह्मचर्यापरिग्रहाः व्रतं ।
अनुव्रतधारी गृहस्थः श्रावकः स्मृतः ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
ahiṃsā-satyāsteya-brahmacaryāparigrahāḥ vrataṃ |
anuvrata-dhārī gṛhasthaḥ śrāvakaḥ smṛtaḥ ||
primary_sources.translation: Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, chastity, and non-possessiveness are vows. The householder who observes these in their minor form is known as a Shravaka.
primary_sources.notes: The Tattvārtha Sūtra (especially around 7.1–7.5 in common numbering) discusses vows for ascetics and householders. The verse here is a composite representation based on standard doctrinal summaries: the five vows and the identification of the lay follower (śrāvaka) as a gṛhastha who observes them as anuvratas. In practice, this category includes Shravikas, who undertake the same minor vows adapted to their circumstances. Exact Sanskrit wording differs slightly among recensions and commentaries; the conceptual content is stable across traditions (Tier A/C).

primary_sources.title: Avasyaka-sutra (Śvetāmbara canon)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to canonical redactors; individual authorship not specified
primary_sources.original_text: पंचपरमेष्ठी-पूजा, गुरुपसेवा, सुत्त-सुयणं, सामायिक्कं, तवो, दाणं—एवमवस्सइयाणि ।
primary_sources.transliteration: pañca-parameṣṭhī-pūjā, guru-upasevā, sutta-suyaṇaṃ, sāmāyikkaṃ, tavo, dāṇaṃ—evam avassaïyāṇi |
primary_sources.translation: Worship of the five supreme beings, service to the Guru, listening to the scriptures, the practice of sāmāyika, austerity, and charity—these are the essential duties.
primary_sources.notes: The Avasyaka-sutra enumerates the six essential duties (ṣaḍ-āvaśyaka) for all Jains, including Shravakas and Shravikas. The Prakrit wording and sequence vary slightly among manuscripts and commentarial traditions. These duties structure daily practice for lay followers and monastics alike, emphasizing worship, scriptural engagement, meditation, austerity, and charity. The text is part of the Śvetāmbara canonical corpus (Tier A), with extensive traditional commentaries (Tier B).

primary_sources.title: Indian Epigraphical Glossary (śrāvikā entry, based on ancient Jain inscriptions)
primary_sources.author: Compiled by epigraphists; individual inscription authors vary
primary_sources.notes: Epigraphical glossaries, drawing on inscriptions in Sanskrit and Prakrit, define "śrāvikā" explicitly as a female lay worshipper. This confirms that the term was used historically to denote women who belonged to the Jain lay community and participated in religious activities. While not a doctrinal text, such epigraphical evidence (Tier C/D) supports the interpretation of Shravika as the female counterpart to Shravaka within the fourfold saṅgha.

misconceptions.myth: A Shravika is simply a passive listener who attends sermons but does not have a defined ethical or spiritual role.
misconceptions.reality: Classical Jain texts describe Shravikas as full participants in the lay path of partial renunciation, bound by the twelve vows, six essential duties, and graded practices of restraint. Listening to teachings is the starting point, but the identity of a Shravika is defined by active practice of ahiṃsā, satya, asteya, brahmacarya, and aparigraha in household life.

misconceptions.myth: Shravika is a purely social or honorific title for any Jain woman, regardless of her commitment to vows or practice.
misconceptions.reality: While the term can be used respectfully in community contexts, doctrinal and epigraphical sources link "śrāvikā" specifically to women who adopt the lay vows and participate in religious observances. The title implies a relationship to the dharma—listening, learning, and practicing—rather than merely belonging to a Jain family by birth.

misconceptions.myth: Shravikas are spiritually inferior to monks and nuns and cannot make meaningful progress toward liberation.
misconceptions.reality: Jain doctrine presents the lay path as a legitimate and necessary stage of spiritual development. Texts like Ratnakaraṇḍa Śrāvakācāra and Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya affirm that sincere lay practice—by Shravakas and Shravikas—reduces karmic bondage and prepares the soul for deeper renunciation. The distinction between lay and monastic paths concerns the degree of abstinence, not the ultimate spiritual goal.

misconceptions.myth: Shravika duties are limited to domestic rituals and have no relevance to ethical decisions in work, society, or modern life.
misconceptions.reality: The core vows and duties of a Shravika—non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, sexual responsibility, and non-possessiveness—apply to all spheres of life, including professional conduct, social engagement, and digital interactions. Contemporary Jain teachers and scholars emphasize that Shravika ethics must be interpreted dynamically, guiding decisions about consumption, environmental impact, business practices, and interpersonal relationships.

misconceptions.myth: Only ascetics are required to study scriptures; Shravikas are expected to focus on ritual and devotion alone.
misconceptions.reality: Scriptural study (svādhyāya) is explicitly listed among the six essential duties for lay followers. Many Shravakācāra texts encourage Shravikas and Shravakas to cultivate right knowledge through regular reading, listening to discourses, and reflection. Devotion and ritual are important, but they are meant to be integrated with understanding and ethical discernment.
